 File Photos Besmellah Zahidi · November 20, 2026 WHO Reports Fourfold Rise in Dengue Cases in Afghanistan
 KABUL, AFGHANISTAN – Suspected dengue cases in Afghanistan increased more than fourfold in October compared with the previous month, with one associated death recorded, the World Health Organization (WHO) said in its latest update , as the country’s healthcare system continues to grapple with funding shortages and operational challenges.
 The WHO recorded 1,675 suspected dengue cases and one associated death between October 4 and 31, a 360.2% increase from 364 suspected cases and no deaths reported in September. The fatality was the first dengue-related death recorded in Afghanistan since January 2026, the report said.
 Meanwhile, according to the report, cases of several other infectious diseases declined in October. Suspected Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever cases fell by 44.1%, confirmed COVID-19 cases by 67.7%, acute watery diarrhea cases by 34.7% and suspected measles cases by 22.6%. Cases of acute respiratory infection with pneumonia decreased by 3.8%.
 Dengue is a viral disease transmitted through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes. While most infections cause mild or moderate symptoms, severe cases can lead to serious complications and become life-threatening, according to the WHO.
 More on this story 
 Local sources have also reported a significant increase in dengue infections across eastern Afghanistan, particularly in Nangarhar province, where two young men reportedly died from the disease. According to the sources, both had been receiving treatment at local hospitals for several weeks before their deaths. One died in Jalalabad city, the provincial capital, while the other died in Momand Dara district.
 The reported increase comes as Afghanistan’s healthcare system continues to face serious challenges following the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021. The withdrawal and reduction of international assistance, the country’s prolonged economic crisis and the return of millions of Afghans from neighboring countries have placed additional pressure on an already fragile health sector.
 Hundreds of health facilities across the country have closed or reduced their operations in recent years, largely because of funding shortages. Restrictions imposed by the Taliban on women’s participation in healthcare and humanitarian work have also affected the delivery of essential services, particularly for women and girls.
 The WHO and other humanitarian organizations have repeatedly warned about the consequences of declining health-sector funding in Afghanistan, calling for sustained international assistance to maintain essential medical services, strengthen disease surveillance and improve the country’s capacity to prevent, detect and respond to infectious disease outbreaks.
